This is a much-needed and clearly well-developed contribution to the field of innovation
intermediation in the (European) space industry.
The article is using desk analysis, surveys and interview data to build a picture of the existing
provision and skills in innovation intermediation across Europe (especially focusing on central and
south-eastern Europe). The findings support existing research pointing to significant differences in
needs and available support, with the dominance of soft skills, networking, etc, and a lack of
support for R&D. (This has been shown in smaller studies already, like my own work: Vidmar
(2019), The Ten Million Euro Question: How Do Innovation Intermediaries Support Smart
Specialization? Croatian Economic Survey. [external resource identifier omitted]
The main challenge of this paper is its reliance on a very narrow set of exclusively EU/Horizonfunded initiatives for the literature review and desk-research data.
Thus, it neglects recent significant research myself and colleagues have done in innovation
intermediation in the space industry (especially in dealing with emerging / non-traditional
contexts).
The key references sorely missing here would be:
Vidmar (2020). Innovation Intermediaries and (Final) Frontiers of High-tech.
Palgrave/Springer. [external resource identifier omitted]
as well as:
Venturini and Verbano (2014). A systematic review of the Space technology transfer literature:
Research synthesis and emerging gaps. Space Policy.
[external resource identifier omitted] 3
In addition, there is little discussion of the significant role of ESA, as it has been well documented
by Mazzucato and Robinson (2016) Market Creation and the European Space Agency. [external resource identifier omitted]




media.esa.int/docs/business_with_esa/Mazzucato_Robinson_Market_creation_and_ESA.pdf 4
All of these develop actionable frameworks and taxonomies to bring together the different
dimensions of the innovation intermediation roles into more simplified structures, specifically
looking at the Space sector, especially Vidmar (2021). Enablers, Equippers, Shapers and Movers: A
typology of innovation intermediaries' interventions and the development of an emergent innovation
system. [external resource identifier omitted]
Some more engagement with this literature, as well as other sources of data on skills and gaps in
the European space industry, is strongly recommended (for example, see this report by Space
Skills Alliance: [external resource identifier omitted]

This paper provides new empirical evidence and knowledge and skills in the space sector for
European countries. I have several suggestions and comments which are listed below.
Main points:
1. The dependent variables are Likert scaled. Ordinary Least squares (OLS) is not appropriate
to analyse the Likert scaled data. Likert scaled variables are usually analysed using the
ordered probit or ordered logit model or structural equation modelling (see a standard
econometrics textbook, for instance Wooldridge or Greene). Given the sample size, I
suggest to use the ordered probit or ordered logit model.
2. The quoted literature only partly motivates the empirical model. This paper is about
competencies and skills in the space industry, and not about performance.
3. The empirical model and the specification are not satisfactory. One type of skill cannot be
related to other types. Of course, different types of skills are correlated. I cannot see the




control variables. Have you included country dummy variables or firm size?
4. Please outline the contribution of the work to the literature a bit more. Please elaborate on
what is already known in the literature and what is the research gap. I also suggest clearly
formulating the specific research questions the study focuses on.
5. The conclusions are very generic. There are a few implications for stakeholders. More work
is needed here.
6. The online survey is not presentative. 62 per cent of the respondents are coming from three
countries. Are the results different for countries in Eastern Europe? Please provide
information on the universe of the respondents (source).
7. There are too many diagrams and tables and very little text. Please look at the study again
and revise it.
Specific comments:
Abstract: Please make the abstract more interesting for the readers. Please be more specific.
“….several interesting insights for the future of the European space innovation have been
identified…” This is too generic.
There are several typos and the language is not always smooth. Example: Countries in the CE and
SE Europe, be they with emerging or existing space…”
Introduction: The paragraph on total factor productivity growth of the CE and SE countries does
not fit.
Please provide descriptive statistics of the dependent and independent variables. I can see that
the means are reported but not the standard deviation.
Please also elaborate on the sampling design (stratified random sampling) and the treatment of
non response.
Figure 3: Please change to a table. A graph based on 15 observations does not look good.
Table 6: add -values.
The decimal system in English is the dot (e.g. 1.0) not the comma (1,0). Please adjust all tables (see
for instance Table 3).
The authors should give information about the software command. The software package (Gretl)
is given, but not the command.

We would like to thank the reviewer for their comments and recommendations
that helped us improve our paper. The manuscript has been revised accordingly in an effort
to address them. The revised manuscript has been resubmitted.
In more detail, the manuscript has been revised to include valuable references from the
reviewer.

We would like to thank the reviewer for their comments and recommendations
that helped us improve our paper. The manuscript has been revised accordingly in an effort
to address them. The revised manuscript has been resubmitted.
In more detail, as the reviewer's suggestion for the analysis of the Likert scaled data. As the
reviewers' comments reached the authors at a point at which the analysis could not be
performed with a more appropriate model, the respective analysis has been removed
entirely from the manuscript. In addition, the literature has been updated based also on the
input of the 2nd Reviewer. In principle, the literature presented in Section 2 "Related Work",
aimed to fuel the generation of the initial baseline framework of skills and knowledge, as
well as the timely need for such an assessment. The authors strongly believe that
performance is an integral part of our rationale for creating a baseline of knowledge and
skills framework, as it supports the fact that knowledge and skills are an essential
contribution to the success of innovation intermediaries' support service delivery towards
local space innovators. To further enrich the flow of the manuscript, the specific research
questions have been introduced in the Introduction, whereas the Results and Discussion
section has been enriched to better outline the contribution of our work to the literature.
Finally, a Limitations section has been introduced to the manuscript to address the
comment on the sample distribution and country representation.

Methods

The approach followed for delivering the envisioned analysis consists of four steps, as can be seen in Figure 1. Starting
with a desk research based on reports and knowledge gained
from previous EU projects, as well as recent literature, so as to
develop an initial baseline framework of the various skills that
competent innovation intermediaries should possess in order
to provide business support services to innovators (Step 1).
Subsequently, we deployed a series of semi-structured interviews with experts in the SE and CE European local ecosystems, gathering feedback to fine-tune and validate the baseline
framework we developed (Step 2). This exercise enabled us to
set a space-related market-driven framework of desired skills
and competencies. At the same time, the main elements of this
framework were transformed into an online survey to investigate in more detail the views and perceptions from both
stakeholder sides, i.e., innovation intermediaries and space
innovators (Step 3). The final step of our approach delved into
a more detailed analysis concerning the skill-sets of innovation
intermediaries needed for leading their innovators to a successful

methodological steps followed.

3.1 Step1: Desk research
We begun our approach by conducting desk research to develop
a baseline framework for our analysis and identify the current
state-of-play in the skill levels and needs of innovation intermediaries in providing business support services to innovators. The desk research relied on specific available reports and
online sources of other relevant projects (EU H2020/FP7

projects) that InnORBIT partnersv have been (or currently are)
involved in (see Table 1). These projects deal with innovation
support aspects, helping innovators at gaining access to tailored
business support services or bringing their innovations to
the market. A particular focus was given to the business and
training needs of innovation intermediaries and innovators in
cutting-edge industries and verticals. By capitalizing on partners’ accumulated knowledge in other projects, we are able to

outline an initial framework of required skills of innovation
intermediaries.

3.2 Step 2: Semi-structured interviews
The second step in our approach further calibrates the initial
baseline framework and distinguishes between the critical
and non-critical skills of innovation intermediaries. The goal
here is to identify any skill areas and dimensions not previously
envisaged in our initial framework (Step 1). Therefore, we validate our initial findings, based on the views of experts belonging in our two stakeholder groups (innovation intermediaries
and innovators). This exercise reveals which specific skills and
skill areas should be included in the questionnaire of the online
survey, fuelling the activities of Step 3. Since detailed information is not always available online, we pursued close consultations with various public and private stakeholders from
the targeted regions via a series of semi-structured interviews.
To start the process, an interview guideline that comprised of a
summary of the InnORBIT project, an overview of the objectives of the interview and a baseline framework to guide the
discussion, was prepared. The baseline framework ensures that
the conversations stay focused on the topic and that no important aspects are neglected, but at the same time, it allows for
sufficient room for discussion and refinement of the framework.
By engaging InnORBIT partners´ networks we identified
highly experienced innovation intermediaries and innovators,
which we sought to interview about their perspectives on innovation intermediaries´ required skills for delivering business
support services, focusing on the space industry dimension
and its applications. Two interview questionnaires were developed, facilitating consultations with the groups of innovators
(namely: entrepreneurs, start-ups, and scale-ups) and innovation
intermediaries, respectively.
During interview sessions, the baseline framework was presented to experts, with a view to defining the types of skills
innovation intermediaries need to possess in order to provide
effective business support to entrepreneurs. Depending on the
stakeholder group, experts were asked to validate the baseline
framework from the point of view of either (i) innovation intermediaries; as providers of support services, or (ii) innovators;
as recipients of such services.
The validation process has been carried out via quantitative
and qualitative means. More specifically, interviewees were
asked to rate the significance of skills categories and specific
skills included in our baseline framework based on a scale
from 1 to 5, with 1 assigned to “not important” skills and 5 to
“absolutely important” skills. A skill is considered validated,
as long as its average rating and its mode (i.e., the value that
appears most frequently in a data set) exceed the value of 3 (average level). This thresholds derives naturally from the design
of the Likert scale response, under which any value above 3
is perceived positively. At the same time, respondents were
requested to identify those skills or skills categories missing
from our baseline framework as well as to highlight any changes
needed in the definition and classification of skills included.

In total, we performed 15 interviews (9 with innovation intermediaries and 6 with innovators across the EU) via digital
means; interviews’ insights are collected, synthesized, and
analysed further, ultimately leading to the update of the initial
baseline framework. The f

ine-tuned version of our baseline
framework built the premises for developing and deploying
an online survey under Step 3.

3.3 Step 3: Online survey
In the third step, we deploy an online survey to reveal the skill
levels of space-related innovation intermediaries based on
(i) their own perceptions and (ii) the perspectives of innovators who received these business support skills and services.
While this exercise has mostly a geographical focus on the ecosystems of CE and SE Europe, we are also keen to capture
the broader perspective of stakeholders from more developed
ecosystems (EU level), who either provide business support
services to innovators in the region of our focus or have business relationships with innovators in the region. Thus, the
broader perspective of our study offers richer insights on the
business support landscape and the desired skills of innovation intermediaries that are currently valued by innovators
and by market forces in space-related domains.
We divide each sub-section of the current manuscript based
on each skill level category that is investigated in the survey,
namely (i) Knowledge in the Space Industry, (ii) Business Assessment Knowledge, (iii) Business Support Skills, (iv) Organisational and Digital Skills, and (v) Soft Skills. To study in-depth
each core skill area, we used a set of well-tailored Likert-scale
survey questions, addressing specific business sub-element of
each core skill area. Specifically, we employed a 5-level scale,
with 1 indicating low levels of skills and 5 indicating high
levels of skills.
The selected skill areas and questions of the survey are based on
the fine-tuned framework developed under Step 2. The survey
was implemented online via a survey tool (i.e. EUSurveyvi) to
ensure a broad and effective data collection process. In particular, two separate and anonymous survey questionnaires were
developed. The first addresses the perceived skills and needs of
innovation intermediaries, namely the perceptions of advisors,
trainers, coaches, and mentors belonging to clusters, incubators,
accelerators and SME support organisations in space-related
and other sectors. The second addresses the views of innovators; we asked them to indicate their experiences and knowledge
received from their participation in training with innovation
intermediaries, and more specifically, we investigate the skill
levels of innovation intermediaries from an innovator’s point
of view. In essence, we analyse the same factor (namely, innovation intermediaries’ skills and needs) from two different
angles: the service provider side (innovation intermediaries) and
the service recipient side (innovators). This approach enables us to reveal any differences in the perceptions of the two
groups under investigation, examine how these perceptions
vary, and extract informed implications for the core objectives

of this study; (i) to identify the available missing skills of innovation intermediaries, and (ii) to reveal the needs of innovators’
ecosystems.
To enhance the outcomes of our research and to reach out to a
sufficient number of suitable intermediaries around Europe, relevant experts from the InnORBIT network (within the project
and external) were invited to complete the survey – these experts
include relevant trainers of innovation intermediaries around
Europe, such as consultancies, accelerators, incubators, and
innovation agencies. On top of that, we disseminated the survey to innovators who are involved in space-related technologies, exploiting mostly the contacts of consortium’s clusters
and start-up networks. The online survey aimed for at least
100 participants for extracting meaningful insightsvii.

3.4 Step 4: analysis
The last part of our approach delves into insights stemming
from the online survey. Our objective was to identify deficit patterns amongst innovation intermediaries (current vs. necessary
skills/knowledge) that need to be addressed via capacity building
services, as well as to use inferential analytics exploring potential relations and patterns to produce intelligence for fine-tuning
the business support services to be provided by space innovation
related local support initiatives.
Survey results were gathered, consolidated, and analysed. We
employed relevant statistical tools (i.e., GRETLviii) to identify patterns and relationships among the different sets of skill
areas. To start, we conducted a correlation analysis, to reveal
how each skill area in our survey is associated with others.
While correlation quantifies the direction and strength of the
relationship between two skill areas, we also introduced and
estimated a multiple linear regression model, based on the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method. By doing so, we assessed
the association among the different skill areas and needs using
survey data. Our statistical approach models the various skill
areas (treating them as a set of variables) through a stochastic
equation of the form:

5 Conclusion

We have synthesized the key inferences that stem from the
online survey, building on the outcomes of the quantile analysis, the correlations among various skill areas, and the regression
analysis we employed. In this section, we present the conclusions of our study concerning the (i) available and missing
skills of local innovation intermediaries with respect to effectively supporting space innovation as well as (ii) needs of
local ecosystems of entrepreneurs, startups, and scale-ups in
terms of successfully driving value from space innovation.
The key insights of this report are summarised below (see also
Figure 20 and Figure 21 for an illustration of the key insights
stemming from this study).
We conclude that innovation intermediaries under investigation
have the adequate capacity to effectively train and support
innovators at improving primarily their organisational skills
and soft skills. Along the same lines, trainers are also competent
at assessing the investment readiness levels of innovators, and
their pitching skills, as well as they can also provide tailored
business support services to innovators. After all, we have identified a positive correlation between the soft skills of innovation intermediaries and their inherent ability to evaluate
the business potential of innovators.

On the other hand, a key finding of this study is that space innovators need to receive better training to improve their business modelling skills, support the management of their business
Intellectual Property, and understand key technologies of the
space market. Based on the latter, space innovators need also
to better identify how specific space technologies can be used
in other domains and industries, while innovation intermediaries, having a more horizontal knowledge on the potential
applications of technological innovations, could act as facilitators in this process. Interestingly, the key role of financing

er, the CE and SE Europe are abundant with talent offering a highly skilled and educated tech workforce with great
potential for space innovation. Over the last twenty years, the
regions of interest have shown positive signs in terms of labour
productivity growth, leading to economic growthii, and therefore converging to the EU average8. The new era and the transformation of many CE and SE European economies require that
innovation will be a key component in their new growth models to foster prosperity even further. More importantly, given

the region, be it support to local innovation intermediaries or

At the same time, it is also essential to ensure that these innovation intermediaries have all the necessary knowledge, skills,
resources and tools in place to effectively organise their local
initiatives to support their portfolio of innovators and enable
them to engage and drive value from space innovation, bringing
the EU at the forefront of the global new space race. Towards this
direction, this manuscript, which covers work performed under
the EU-funded H2020 InnORBIT project (GA No 101004212)iii,

Hence the research questions (RQs) that arise from the analysis of this rapidly evolving section in the CE and SE Europe are
the following:
•	RQ1: Which are the most essential skills and knowledge innovation intermediaries should possess to
effectively train and provide business support services to innovators active in the space and space-related
sectors?
•	RQ2: What is the perceived maturity of these skills
and knowledge from the innovation intermediaries’ and
innovators’ perspectives?
•	RQ3: What are the elements of a capacity building programme for innovation intermediaries towards improving their skills and knowledge to more effectively
support their local ecosystem?
Towards addressing these questions, the present study offers
novel findings to the existing literature that can be organised into 4 main pillars. First, we consider the implications for
potential training programmes of an extensive analysis of the
current skill levels and knowledge gaps of members of innovation intermediaries. We offer new insights for the market-driven
design and development of new initiatives to build the business skills and space knowledge capacity of trainers, coaches
and innovation advisors in the CE and SE Europe and beyond.
Secondly, and in line with the previous pillar, we also offer
practical suggestions for new courses and training content
that could be considered in future capacity building initiatives in the area. In parallel, our third pillar of findings deals
with the investigation of the current perceptions of innovators in
the CE and SE Europe and the analysis of their inherent needs
in terms of business support. By doing so, we provide new
insights and suggestions on the desired content for the design
and development of new business support programmes that
will target space innovators in the CE and SE Europe and
beyond. Lastly, our study also contributes to design tools for
supporting space entrepreneurshi

f an effective innovation
intermediary.
Piispanen et al. (2017)13 indicate that entrepreneurs should
possess core business knowledge and skills to enhance their
business development. In a similar vein, Anwar (2018)14 identifies the Business Model Innovation (BMI) as a core driver for
an innovator’s better performance, influencing positively its
comparative advantage, especially in growing industries like

the space industry. Many studies also pinpoint that entrepreneurship is significantly boosted when innovators adopt new
digital technologies, upgrade their digital capabilities, and follow a concrete digital strategy, helping them to become innovation leaders (Khin and Ho, 201915, Ismail et al., 201716, Sousa
and Rocha, 201917). These findings suggest that digital and
organisational skills should constitute a core area of the effective
innovation intermediary.
Within the space domain, clusters, the most common form of
innovation intermediary, are an integral aspect that evolves
rapidly along the space economy, especially considering
that its development is mainly based on dispersed interventions in supporting innovation, rather than a unified national
programme18. In a recent thorough international comparison on
space cluster development19, the authors have found that “skills
are ‘sticky’ and drive the space economy in the long term”.
Nevertheless, in most if not all cases examined, the space clusters are highly dependent on external entities, such as universities, and even in huge organisations, such as NASA, there
is a risk of skills shortage due to an ageing workforce. With all
of that in mind, it is difficult to imagine how space clusters can
effectively support innovation without being up-skilled or reskilled, not only to remain competitive within an erupting market, but also to act as drivers and enablers for the innovator
ecosystem. Moreover, according to the Space Skills Alliance20,
SMEs in the downstream sector, are in need of a more diverse
skill set in their workforce, which in most cases cannot be found,
mainly due to the lack of resources to invest in up-skilling,
but also due to the limited capacity of the available trainers.
There are sparse findings in the literature regarding skill and
knowledge capacity assessment in the space industry. In an
extensive systematic literature review in 201421, have analysed in
depth the international technology transfer trends in the space
industry. Although they have identified multiple dimensions,
they have not investigated the capacity of the involved actors
to effectively support their ecosystems, including technology
transfer support.
Focusing more on the actual job market, the Space Skills Alliance has also created a competencies taxonomy22, including extended knowledge and skills aspects. According to their
findings, which were based on 812 early career UK space job
adverts, a taxonomy of five categories has been created to
describe the competencies required from the space industry in
the UK. Namely: Traits, Knowledge, Technical skills, Transferable skills, and Qualifications. This taxonomy covers a wide
range of necessary knowledge and skills areas, however, its
focus is on the overall workforce of the UK space industry, and
not on the role of innovation intermediaries as support pillars.
A recent skills gap assessment in Australia23, revealed quite interesting findings, starting with the fact that there is a clear shift
from technical to soft skills and space sector enabling skills
(specialised business, finance, regulatory, legal skills), which
are even considered critical for the current market. This,
along with the shortages identified in almost all of the skills


categories in this study, highlights the necessity for up-skilling and
knowledge transfer. Going in more depth in the analysis of
innovation intermediaries, their activities, strategies, roles and
impacts, Vizmar24 thoroughly analysed the Scottish New Space
Sector, highlighting the need for investment, networking, and
capacity-building support, while redefining (potentially) the
role of innovation intermediaries for driving innovation in their
local ecosystem.
The existing literature, although not specifically and in detail,
addresses the issue of intermediaries’ skills and knowledge needs in the space industry, offering a variety of desired
attributes and skill sets that an effective business trainer/coach
should possess. Despite the several factors that could be considered in a framework model for the assessment of the skill
perceptions of such trainers, we can mostly identify four key
aspects. Namely, these aspects refer to the business skills of
intermediaries, their capacity to support innovators at embracing digital transformation and designing a digital strategy,
as well as their ability to improve the soft skill of innovators and their networking with relevant innovation actors. This
analysis of our framework model for intermediaries’ skills
and knowledge is further upended by also studying the key
insights stemming from other relevant EU-funded R&D
projects that the authors have been engaged with (see Table 1),
focusing on innovation and business support. It is important to
state at this point that the introduced framework is not aiming
to propose a new taxonomy or to get into a detailed analysis of
the knowledge and skills assessed, but mainly to offer a better
understanding of the current capacity of innovation intermediaries and pathways towards improvements for effectively
supporting their ecosystem.

3 Methods

The approach followed for delivering the envisioned analysis consists of four steps, as can be seen in Figure 1. Starting
with a desk research based on reports and knowledge gained
from previous EU projects, as well as recent literature, so as to
develop an initial baseline framework of the various skills that
competent innovation intermediaries should possess in order
to provide business support services to innovators (Step 1).
Subsequently, we deployed a series of semi-structured interviews with experts in the local SE and CE European ecosystems,
gathering feedback to fine-tune and validate the baseline framework we developed (Step 2). This exercise enabled us to set a
space-related market-driven framework of desired skills and
competencies. At the same time, the main elements of this
framework were transformed into an online survey to investigate in more detail the views and perceptions from both stakeholder sides, i.e., innovation intermediaries and space innovators
(Step 3). The final step of our approach delved into a more
detailed analysis concerning the skill-sets of innovation intermediaries needed for leading their innovators to a successful journey into space innovation, as well as the perceived
business needs of innovators in the space industry, via
analysing our survey results (Step 4). The following sections,
provide a more elaborate description of the methodological
steps followed.

To enhance the outcomes of our research and to reach out to

The last part of our approach delves into insights stemming
from the online survey. Our objective was to identify deficit patterns amongst innovation intermediaries (current vs. necessary

fine-tuning the business support services to be provided by
space innovation related local support initiatives.
Survey results were gathered, consolidated, and analysed to
extract insights on the skills and knowledge areas of innovation
intermediaries that require empowerement to effectively support
their local ecosystem to leverage space innovation and beyond.

While the presented methodology for assessing the knowledge and skill needs of innovation ecosystems in the CE and
SE European space sector is considered thorough, its results
have certain limitations, which warrant discussion to enhance
the transparency and validity of our findings. These limitations pertain to the sample size of participating experts and the
representativeness of respondents.

5 Conclusion

In this section, we present the conclusions of our study concerning the (i) provision of a knowledge and skill assessment
framework for space innovation support; (ii) available and
missing skills of local innovation intermediaries with respect
to effectively supporting space innovation; and (iii) needs of
local ecosystems of entrepreneurs, start-ups, and scale-ups in
terms of successfully driving value from space innovation.

The paper presents robust empirical studies aimed at identifying the requisite knowledge and
skills for startups in the space industry. The methodology employed to discern these variables is
commendably logical, systematically delving deeper at each step. Still, there are noteworthy areas
that warrant further consideration:
1. Geographic Distribution of Samples: I observed a predominant representation of respondents
from central-eastern and south-eastern European countries, with limited inclusion from western
European countries or those traditionally associated with the space industry. While the paper
acknowledges this in the title, it remains unclear in the main body whether this distribution is
intentional or constrained by accessibility to respondents. This discrepancy could potentially
impact the perceived significance of various indicators in "space industry knowledge," such as
"relevant national, EU, and international regulations" and "national policy."
2. Initial Baseline Framework: The foundation derived from desktop research on EU projects and
the literature is commendable; however, additional elaboration would enhance understanding.
Clarification is needed on why certain variables are grouped in specific categories, particularly as
some variables lack clarity. For example, the rationale behind placing "entrepreneurship
incentives" under "space industry knowledge" requires further justification.
3. Sector-Specific Considerations: While the paper is centred on the space sector, it appears that
the study's design, from research methodology to identified indicators, could be applicable to any
industrial sector. Is there a bespoke consideration tailored explicitly for the space industry? Even
the indicators in "space industry knowledge" seem more general than space-specific, giving the
impression that the study is designed for technology startups in general and then applied to the
space sector as a case study.
4. Findings Exploration: The paper's findings, especially the substantial disparities among experts,
innovation intermediaries, and innovators, are intriguing. However, delving deeper into the
underlying reasons behind these gaps would enrich the paper and provide a more comprehensive
understanding.
